unit.title: Exponents, Roots, and Power Structure
unit.act: Act VI - Leaving constant additive change
unit.role: Introduce repeated multiplication, its inverse questions, and the first nonlinear families.
unit.governingQuestion: How do repeated multiplication and roots create new structures?
unit.storyArc: Exponent laws are derived from repeated factors; zero and negative exponents preserve those laws; roots reverse powers; simple power equations and graphs reveal behavior unlike lines.
outcomes: Interpret integer exponents and negative bases.
Interpret roots and solve simple power equations.
Compare linear, quadratic, cubic, and root patterns.
unit.investigation: Compare additive and power-based scaling in area, volume, and measurement contexts.
unit.mastery: Students justify exponent laws from repeated multiplication and solve mixed exact power/root equations.

lessons.title: Exponents as repeated multiplication
lessons.outcome: Distinguish base, exponent, factors, and value.

opening.prompt: Build area and volume from repeated side lengths.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make exponents as repeated multiplication necessary.

exposition: Distinguish base, exponent, factors, and value. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In exponents as repeated multiplication, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Repeated-factor chain. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Square/cube geometry. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.
